name: xxHash
workload: Bandwidth (GB/s) and small-data velocity of hashing in-RAM buffers, measured with the project's open-source bench program (tests/bench).
claimed_speedup: XXH3 (AVX2) 59.4 GB/s vs City64 22.0 GB/s (~2.7x) and City128 21.7 GB/s (~2.7x), both derived from page data; also vs MurmurHash Murmur3 (32-bit) 3.9 GB/s (~15.2x, derived from page data; note Murmur3 row is the 32-bit variant, so not a perfectly matched width comparison against XXH3's 64/128-bit output). Small-data velocity: XXH3 133.1 vs City64 76.6, vs Murmur3 56.1.
tradeoffs: XXH3/XXH128 use vectorized (SSE2/AVX2) code paths so peak numbers depend on target ISA; not a cryptographic hash (explicitly documented); 32-bit XXH32 exists for constrained targets but is far slower than XXH3.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own bench program) though methodology, compiler, flags, and CPU are fully stated, meeting Tier A. Table does not include std::hash (a listed baseline) directly, only CityHash and MurmurHash competitors; std::hash implementations vary by stdlib and are generally FNV/Murmur-derived so real-world gaps track the Murmur3 row.

name: wyhash
workload: Bulk hashing speed (MiB/sec) and cycles/hash over SMHasher's standard corpus, run on the default reference machine.
claimed_speedup: wyhash 22,640.53 MiB/s vs xxh3 20,853.74 MiB/s (~1.09x, derived from page data); vs City64 14,390.09 MiB/s (~1.57x, derived from page data); vs Murmur3A 3,027.30 MiB/s (~7.5x, derived from page data).
hardware: Default reference machine: AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz (per the linked sortable results table); compiler/flags not stated in the README table itself
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; default hash of Zig, V, Nim, and Go (since 1.17); used in abseil's low_level_hash.h and Windows Terminal
tradeoffs: No patent grant (Unlicense/public-domain dedication). Author states wyhash/wyrand are not fully 64-bit collision resistant (~62 bits) and wyrand can fail PractRand on very long (32TB) streams. wyhash's own README states the project 'has evolved into rapidhash', its successor, so new adopters are steered elsewhere.
caveats: wyhash's own README/repo contains no benchmark table; the numeric win over xxHash comes from the independent rurban/smhasher shootout, a well-known third-party suite, which states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) but not compiler/flags in the text reviewed, capping this at Tier B rather than A. Margin over xxh3 is narrow (~9%) and workload/CPU dependent; other CPUs in the same suite's linked tables may reorder these two.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash README (no benchmark table) -> github.com/rurban/smhasher README (hash function speed table)

name: Zstandard (zstd)
workload: In-memory compression/decompression speed and ratio on the Silesia compression corpus, single-thread, using lzbench.
claimed_speedup: zstd 1.5.7 -1: 510 MB/s compression, 1550 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.896 vs zlib 1.3.1 -1: 105 MB/s compression, 390 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.743 (~4.9x faster compression, ~4.0x faster decompression, derived from page data, at a better ratio). vs brotli 1.1.0 -1: 290 MB/s / 425 MB/s, ratio 2.883 (zstd ~1.8x faster compression, ~3.6x faster decompression, derived from page data, comparable ratio). zstd --fast=4: 665 MB/s / 2050 MB/s vs zlib -1 (~6.3x / ~5.3x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 14.2.0 (via lzbench's standard build; exact optimization flags not individually enumerated in the README)
stars_or_usage: 27.9k stars; reference implementation of RFC 8878, used in Linux kernel, Chromium, FreeBSD, PostgreSQL, and many package managers
tradeoffs: Speed/ratio is tunable via level and --fast=# negative levels; higher levels trade speed for ratio. Dual-licensed (BSD or GPLv2) so usable in both permissive and copyleft contexts. Table does not include xz (a listed baseline) directly, only zlib, brotli, and other fast codecs.
caveats: Benchmark tool (lzbench) is open source and third-party-run but numbers are reported first-party in the project's own README; compiler version, CPU, and OS are stated but exact compile flags are not spelled out beyond 'compiled with gcc 14.2.0', so this is treated as Tier A (reproducible: code, compiler, and CPU model are all identified) rather than C.

name: LZ4
workload: Single-thread in-memory compression/decompression speed and ratio on the Silesia corpus, using lzbench.
claimed_speedup: LZ4 default (v1.9.0): 780 MB/s compression, 4970 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.101 vs zlib deflate 1.2.11 -1: 100 MB/s compression, 415 MB/s decompression, ratio 2.730 (~7.8x faster compression, ~12.0x faster decompression, derived from page data, at a lower ratio). vs Snappy 1.1.4: 565 MB/s / 1950 MB/s, ratio 2.091 (LZ4 ~1.38x faster compression, ~2.55x faster decompression, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC v8.2.0 (via lzbench's standard build; exact optimization flags not individually enumerated in the README)
stars_or_usage: 12.1k stars; used in Linux kernel, ZFS, FreeBSD, and many package/container systems
tradeoffs: Lower compression ratio than zlib/zstd in exchange for very high speed, especially decompression; LZ4_HC trades compression speed for ratio while keeping decompression speed constant; acceleration factor tunable.
caveats: License is mixed: the `lib/` directory (the actual codec) is BSD-2-Clause, while other files including the CLI are GPL-2.0-or-later — record accordingly if only the library is embedded. Benchmark tool (lzbench) is open source but numbers reported first-party in the README; compiler version, CPU, and OS are stated though exact flags are not individually listed, so treated as Tier A.

name: liburing
workload: fio random-read IOPS with 1KB blocks across 4 files, 8 CPUs running 72 fio jobs, iodepth=8; tested both direct I/O on NVMe (uncached) and buffered I/O with a hot page cache; a separate single-CPU 512-byte test on Intel Optane measured throughput and latency.
claimed_speedup: Direct I/O (uncached NVMe): io_uring 1,417,000-1,486,000 IOPS vs linux-aio 1,322,000 IOPS (~1.07-1.12x, derived from page data) and vs synchronous read/write 814,000 IOPS (~1.74-1.83x, derived from page data). Buffered I/O (hot cache): io_uring 5,024,000 IOPS vs linux-aio 4,127,000 (~1.22x, derived from page data) and vs synchronous 4,906,000 (~1.02x, derived from page data). Optane single-CPU: io_uring 346 MB/s / 1,470us vs linux-aio 330 MB/s / 1,549us (author states ~5% faster). Author summary: 'Both io_uring and linux-aio are around twice as fast as the synchronous read interface, which in turn is twice as fast as the thread pool approach employed by posix-aio'.
hardware: 8 CPUs (exact model not stated) with NVMe storage; separate single-CPU test on Intel Optane. Kernel version and fio version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 3.8k stars; the standard userspace helper library for Linux io_uring, used by fio, QEMU, RocksDB, ScyllaDB/Seastar, and many other async-I/O consumers
tradeoffs: Linux-only (5.1+ kernel, more features on newer kernels); API is substantially more complex than read/write or epoll; io_uring has had a number of kernel-side CVEs, leading some distros/hardened environments (e.g. some container platforms, ChromeOS, and Google's production fleet historically) to disable or restrict it by default. One small vendored kernel header is GPL-with-Linux-syscall-note-exception rather than the LGPL/MIT dual license covering the rest of the repo.
caveats: The canonical evidence (Jens Axboe's 'Efficient IO with io_uring' paper at kernel.dk/io_uring.pdf) could not be opened this session due to a TLS certificate/hostname mismatch on kernel.dk, and an LWN.net article covering the same era explicitly states no benchmark numbers had been published yet at that time. Used instead a well-known independent (ScyllaDB) blog benchmark; it names the fio methodology and workload precisely but omits exact CPU model, kernel version, fio version, and compiler flags, so capped at Tier B. Gains over libaio are modest (~7-22%) and workload/queue-depth dependent; the larger win is over synchronous read/write and especially thread-pool POSIX-aio.
